Orin perched on the stool in the lesson booth, the mandolin clamped in his grip, his right wrist throbbing from twenty minutes of tremolo that kept seizing up. Rosin dust hung in the air, and the cold tea beside the metronome had skinned over. Through the glass he saw the owner leaning on the counter, thumbing her phone, a ring of keys dangling from her other hand. He slid off the stool and tapped the door open.

"Hi, sorry to bother you—I'm trying to build endurance for tremolo but my wrist locks up; can you show me the relaxed grip?"

Pallavi glanced at her watch before she glanced at him. "I actually don't teach, I just manage the shop; you'd want to check the teacher schedule on the board."

"The board says all instructors are booked; I just need a quick tip on wrist angle before I leave."

"Honestly, the DVDs in that rack are better than any quick tip I could give you." She nodded at the stack on the counter without lifting her eyes from the screen.

Orin rubbed the sore tendon. "I've watched the videos; I need to know if my anchor point on the bridge is causing the tension."

"It's probably just muscle memory; you'll outgrow it with time and repetition." The keys clinked once against her palm.

"I'm losing time, not building it—does lowering the pick height help or hinder the speed?"

"Everyone's different; I'd stick to what feels natural rather than guessing heights."

He flexed his fingers, the knuckles pale. "Natural feels like cramping after five seconds; is there a warm-up stretch you recommend first?"

Pallavi checked her watch again. "Look, I'm closing up in five minutes; try the warm-up app they recommend online."

"The app is broken; one last thing—do you rotate the forearm or flick from the knuckles?"

The mandolins on the wall caught the dim light as she stepped toward the switch panel. "I really have to lock the doors now; just read the back of those DVD cases."

Orin picked up the top case and turned it over. "The cases just list tracks; you're dodging the technical question entirely."

"The technical answer is in the book; I'm turning off the lights." Her hand rested on the first switch, and the front half of the store went dark.

He set the case down square on the stack and lifted his mandolin by the neck. "Fine—thanks for the redirection."

"Goodnight." The lock turned behind him before he reached the door.

The package room is a windowless concrete box behind the residential lobby, illuminated by harsh LED strips that cast long, sterile shadows across rows of gray smart lockers. The air smells of ozone and damp cardboard. One locker, unit 404, has its red error light pulsing steadily, a rhythmic heartbeat of failure. Renzo stands with his phone in one hand and a bulky envelope in the other, shoulders tense. He needs a quick fix—either a reboot sequence or a code override—to drop off a thesis draft before his advisor’s deadline. He views Polina as a technical peer, assuming her presence near the kiosk implies authority.

Polina, however, is leaning against the far wall, scrolling through her phone with one hand while holding a half-eaten granola bar in the other. She is not staff; she is merely waiting for a friend who is twenty minutes late. She resents the interruption, her body language closed off, eyes fixed on her screen even as Renzo approaches. She wants to disengage immediately. The interaction turns on two concrete objects: the QR code scanner on the locker’s touchscreen, which Renzo keeps tapping fruitlessly, and Polina’s phone, which she checks every few seconds, signaling her imminent departure. Renzo pushes for specific troubleshooting steps; Polina deflects with vague suggestions to contact IT or try a different locker, never offering actual technical aid.

Renzo stabbed a finger at the touchscreen, then pulled it back when nothing changed. "Okay, just one second—does the red light mean network drop or sensor misalignment?"

"It probably means the locker is full; I'd just leave it with the concierge." Her phone lit again and she tilted it away from him.

He nodded at the open compartment, its empty steel mouth. "It's not full, the compartment is open. I need a technical answer, not a workaround."

Polina pushed off the wall, thumb already typing. "Look, my friend's here, so I really have to go; try calling IT."

The door sighed shut. The red light kept pulsing.

The emergency app testing lab is a windowless box of gray carpet and server hum, lit by the cold glow of six monitor walls displaying a simulated wildfire spreading across a topographic map. The air conditioning rattles with a rhythmic shudder, fighting the heat generated by the GPU clusters. A whiteboard on the far wall is cluttered with failed log entries, red markers streaking through timestamps. Sawyer sits at the central workstation, fingers hovering over a mechanical keyboard, eyes darting between the code terminal and Meera’s tablet. He wears a stained hoodie and has been awake since 4 a.m. debugging a notification latency spike that is causing test subjects to miss evacuation alerts. He needs a concrete method to isolate whether the failure is in the push gateway or the client-side receiver.

Meera stands by the door, one hand on the handle, phone already in her ear but muted. She is wearing a crisp blazer that looks out of place in the lab’s grime, signaling she just arrived from a meeting she is eager to rejoin. She checks her watch every twenty seconds. To her, Sawyer is a nuisance blocking her exit from a mandatory but irrelevant safety briefing she was only dragged into because her badge was in the sector. She wants to vanish into the hallway. The conversation hinges on two objects: the jagged latency graph flashing on the main screen and a physical keycard holder hanging from Meera’s neck, which she keeps adjusting as if preparing to swipe out. Sawyer pushes for technical specifics; Meera offers bureaucratic redirects, citing logs, admins, and protocols she refuses to explain. The tension rises as Sawyer realizes she won’t help, and Meera’s deflections grow sharper, focused entirely on her imminent departure.

The church basement canning kitchen smells of boiled fruit and sterilized glass, a thick, cloying sweetness clinging to the linoleum. Steam fogs the small, high windows, and the hum of the industrial dishwasher competes with the distant muffled sound of the choir practice upstairs. Long folding tables are stacked with mason jars of strawberry and apricot jam, their lids still warm. Whitney stands near the end of a table, a stack of blank white label sheets and a roll of clear tape in her hands. She is dressed for a weekend of grading, her posture rigid with the need to get this task over with before dinner. She wants a quick, definitive answer on regulatory compliance for the charity sale—specifically, whether they need batch codes or expiration dates. She is polite but her impatience simmers just beneath the surface; she values efficiency and resists small talk or deflection.

Ulric leans against the sink, drying a jar with a rag that hasn’t been washed in hours. He is wearing a stained apron over a suit that was wrinkled before he arrived. He checks his watch not out of necessity, but as a rhythmic signal of his desire to leave. He resents the extra duty assigned to him and treats Whitney’s questions as interruptions to his mental departure. He knows exactly what the rules are—he helped write the parish newsletter last year—but he actively refuses to share that knowledge. His replies are short, polite, and utterly useless, designed to redirect Whitney toward people who aren’t there or resources she doesn’t have time to check. He wants to be anywhere else, preferably in a car, and uses bureaucratic vagueness as a shield to keep the conversation from gaining momentum. The conversation turns on two concrete objects: the stack of blank labels and a discarded copy of the local health department’s guide sitting under a pot of peeling jam.

Ulric leaned against the sink, working a gray rag around the rim of an apricot jar. He turned his wrist to look at his watch, then at the door. "I'm not sure offhand; the health inspector usually handles those details during walkthroughs."

"I'm trying to print them now. Is there a standard format you recommend?"

"You might check the parish office; they keep the last year's forms in the filing cabinet." He set the jar down and picked up another.

Whitney tapped the label stack against the table edge. "The office is locked until Tuesday. I need to know tonight so the ink doesn't dry out."

"If you're in a rush, maybe just hand-write the dates; it's less formal." His apron was streaked with jam, and the suit beneath it had never been pressed.

"Hand-written labels get rejected. I need to know the rule, not a workaround."

"The rule changes every few months; best to ask the lead coordinator tomorrow."

"The coordinator is out of town. Are you saying I should just guess?"

"I wouldn't guess; I'd wait for official guidance to avoid liability." He glanced at his watch again.

Whitney's eyes went to a pot of peeling jam at the far end, a creased pamphlet pinned beneath it. "Waiting isn't an option. Does the guide under the pot say anything?"

"That copy is outdated; relying on it could cause more issues than it solves." He did not look toward it.

She lifted the labels an inch. "So I have to reprint these? Just yes or no, Ulric."

"If you reprint them, make sure to double-check the font size first." The rag squeaked against glass.

"You're deflecting. Is there a specific section in the county code?"

"It's buried in the subsections; someone with more time should look it up."

"I am the person with time right now. Where do I start?"

"Start by contacting the health department directly; they're helpful on the phone." He hung the rag over the faucet and reached for his keys on the sill.

Whitney's thumb pressed a dent into the tape roll. "Their line has been busy for an hour. Is there a shortcut?"

"No shortcut; compliance requires following the full process carefully."

A breath left her through her nose. She slid the labels under her arm and pulled her phone from her pocket. "Fine. I'll call them again. Thanks for your time."

"You're welcome; good luck with the printing." He was already crossing toward the stairs, apron strings trailing, the choir swelling as he opened the door.

The children’s theater wardrobe loft is a cramped, dusty sanctuary suspended above the main stage, accessible only by a rattling metal ladder. Afternoon light filters through grimy skylights, catching clouds of suspended glitter that drift like slow snow over racks of moth-eaten velvet and polyester sequins. The air smells of stale sweat, hairspray, and the sharp, chemical tang of fabric stiffeners. Talulah stands on a wobbly step stool, holding a pair of translucent, net-like fairy wings that currently droop like wet laundry. She wears paint-splattered overalls and looks exhausted, her eyes scanning Urielis with desperate hope. She needs a chemical solution—specifically, how to use diluted Mod Podge or a commercial starch to give the lace structure without making it brittle enough to snap when the actor flaps their arms. She wants a recipe: part A to part B, dry time, flexibility test.

Urielis, a senior fabric sculptor whose reputation precedes them, sits on a milk-crate throne piled with costume repairs they aren’t currently touching. Their phone is propped open against a spool of red thread, displaying a text thread they are clearly more invested in. Urielis’s shoulders are rolled back in a posture of practiced disinterest. They view Talulah’s question as an intrusion on their personal downtime. Urielis knows exactly how to stiffen lace—they’ve done it a hundred times—but offering the answer would require engagement, which is the last thing they want. Their goal is to deflect Talulah to someone else, anywhere else, without admitting incompetence or willingness to help.

The conversation will pivot on two specific items: a jar of half-empty, crusty white glue on a high shelf that Talulah points to as a potential resource, and the sewing machine in the corner that Urielis casually mentions as being "broken" or "in use" to justify not demonstrating the technique. Urielis will repeatedly suggest Talulah ask the costume director or check the internet, while Talulah presses for the specific ratio that prevents cracking.

The stormwater demonstration bay sits on the edge of the campus research park, a gravel island surrounded by manicured lawn. It is mid-afternoon, the air thick with the metallic tang of recent rain and wet asphalt. The pavement is a mosaic of interlocking concrete pavers and porous asphalt sections, still glistening from a morning downpour. A steel signpost leans slightly, listing flow rates in faded white paint. Mirek stands on the wet concrete apron, notebook balanced on his forearm, staring at the sample section of the demonstration. He wears a yellow rain shell that’s seen better days, hair plastered to his forehead. He needs to know if crushed granite or recycled concrete aggregate offers better infiltration for his thesis site; he wants a definitive recommendation based on particle size distribution. He is polite but visibly vibrating with the urge to get this over with.

Safa leans against the hood of a parked SUV three yards away, arms crossed, looking at the sky rather than Mirek. She is wearing a field jacket with a different department’s logo and holds a half-eaten sandwich in one hand. She is not a researcher here; she is waiting for a ride from the maintenance crew. Every time Mirek speaks, her eyes flick to her phone, which rests face-up on the car’s roof. She resents the interruption, sensing a technical deep-dive she has no expertise in and no desire to fake. Her goal is minimal engagement, maximum distance. The conversation pivots around the open aggregate storage bin nearby and the spec sheet tucked into Mirek’s notebook, both of which Safa will reference only to dismiss them.
dialogue:
Mirek: Safa, quick question—do you prefer crushed granite or recycled concrete for the top layer aggregate?
Safa: Honestly, I’m just waiting for the truck, but the landscape crew handles that stuff.
Mirek: I need a material spec for my design, not a referral. Which drains faster?
Safa: Depends on the soil compaction; you should ask the civil engineering dept.
Mirek: I’m in civil engineering. Just tell me if the angularity of granite matters here.
Safa: I think so, but I don’t design drains; I just drive the mower sometimes.
Mirek: The mower doesn’t help with hydraulic conductivity. Is the bin over there clean?
Safa: That bin’s been sitting since spring; better check with procurement.
Mirek: Procurement won’t know the permeability class. Granite or recycled concrete?
Safa: Recycled is cheaper, but I really need to get going, sorry.
Mirek: Cheaper isn’t the metric. I need the void ratio comparison.
Safa: Void ratio sounds like a textbook thing; ask your advisor, he knows.
Mirek: My advisor sent me to you because you built this demo bay last year.
Safa: I drove the roller; I didn’t pick the stones, and my ride’s here.
Mirek: So you have zero data on which aggregate performed better?
Safa: Zero, and I’m getting in the truck; good luck with the thesis.

The pavers around him still glistened, and the whole bay smelled of washed gravel and tar. Three yards off, Safa leaned against the hood of an SUV with a sandwich in one hand, eyes on the clouds.

"Safa, quick question—do you prefer crushed granite or recycled concrete for the top layer aggregate?"

Her gaze dropped to the phone resting face-up on the roof of the car, then lifted again. "Honestly, I'm just waiting for the truck, but the landscape crew handles that stuff."

Mirek tugged the spec sheet a half-inch out of his notebook and pushed it back in. "I need a material spec for my design, not a referral. Which drains faster?"

"Depends on the soil compaction; you should ask the civil engineering dept." She took a bite of the sandwich and chewed slowly.

"I'm in civil engineering." A drop slid from his hair down the side of his nose. "Just tell me if the angularity of granite matters here."

"I think so, but I don't design drains; I just drive the mower sometimes." Her thumb nudged the phone's screen awake, then let it dim.

Mirek glanced at the steel signpost, its faded flow rates running down the post. "The mower doesn't help with hydraulic conductivity. Is the bin over there clean?"

Safa tipped her chin toward the open aggregate bin without looking at it. "That bin's been sitting since spring; better check with procurement."

"Procurement won't know the permeability class." He shifted his weight, and the wet concrete squeaked under his boots. "Granite or recycled concrete?"

"Recycled is cheaper, but I really need to get going, sorry." She folded the sandwich wrapper over what was left of it.

"Cheaper isn't the metric." His pen hovered over a blank line. "I need the void ratio comparison."

Safa glanced at the road beyond the lawn, where nothing had appeared yet. "Void ratio sounds like a textbook thing; ask your advisor, he knows."

"My advisor sent me to you because you built this demo bay last year."

Somewhere past the research park a diesel engine rumbled closer. Safa straightened off the hood and pocketed her phone. "I drove the roller; I didn't pick the stones, and my ride's here."

Mirek took a step toward her, notebook still raised. "So you have zero data on which aggregate performed better?"

A white maintenance truck rolled onto the gravel and stopped, its wipers swiping once. Safa pulled open the passenger door. "Zero, and I'm getting in the truck; good luck with the thesis."

The door shut. Mirek stood on the glistening pavers with his pen over the page, while the truck's tires crunched out across the gravel.

The bakery counter is a long slab of stained maple, still cool to the touch despite the ambient heat radiating from the open ovens behind it. It is 4:30 a.m. The air is thick with the scent of blooming yeast and scorched sugar, a heavy, sweet humidity that clings to the throat. Fluorescent lights buzz overhead, reflecting off the chrome pastry displays which are currently empty save for a single, lonely tray of day-old croissants. The floor is scuffed concrete, sticky in patches where dough was dropped hours ago. Nerea stands on the customer side, clutching a crumpled notebook and her phone, the screen glowing with an open blog draft. She is vibrating with caffeine and anxiety, wearing a thrifted apron over her jeans. She wants validation—or at least a definitive rule—about the ethics of digitizing her grandmother’s handwritten recipe cards. She believes sharing the recipe is necessary to grow her business, but fears it betrays the family secret. Her disposition makes her push for a quick, binary answer: safe or unsafe. She has no patience for philosophical waxing.

Bosco leans against the back counter, scrolling through emails on his phone. He is wearing a pristine white chef’s coat that looks too big for him, sleeves rolled up to reveal forearms tense with the urge to move. He has a shift starting in forty minutes at the corporate chain down the street, and he is already mentally clocking out of this family-run hole-in-the-wall. He resents being asked for advice on branding because he views tradition as a shackle he is desperately trying to escape. He does not care about Nerea’s dilemma; he cares about the fifteen minutes left on his break. His disposition manifests as short, dismissive deflections. He will not answer the ethical question because he has no opinion worth giving, only a desire to be elsewhere. He redirects her to the internet, to customers, or to generic concepts, offering no substance. The conversation will turn on two objects: Nerea’s phone, displaying the recipe, and Bosco’s watch, which he checks every few seconds. The tension lies in Nerea’s need for a concrete boundary and Bosco’s refusal to provide any wall at all.
dialogue:
Nerea: I’m posting my grandmother’s sourdough starter recipe online to build traffic, but does that cheapen the family tradition?
Bosco: You should ask your actual customers if they care about the history or just the loaf.
Nerea: I need a professional opinion, not a poll. Is it disrespectful to publish a private family recipe for gain?
Bosco: Respect is subjective; you’re the one setting the brand guidelines, not me.
Nerea: So you’re saying there’s no inherent ethical cost? I just want a yes or no.
Bosco: There’s no universal rule book for bakery ethics; you’re the boss of this place.
Nerea: I’m not asking who’s boss, I’m asking if you think it devalues the craft.
Bosco: Devaluation depends on your sales numbers, which I don’t have access to.
Nerea: This is vague. If you were me, would you keep the starter secret or share it?
Bosco: I’m not in your position, so I’d make a different choice entirely.
Nerea: That’s a deflection. I’m paying rent on this space using this recipe. Is it theft of heritage?
Bosco: Heritage isn’t legal currency; you’re worrying about ghosts, not margins.
Nerea: Margins are fine if the soul is gone. Do you believe soul exists in a recipe?
Bosco: Soul is marketing speak; flour is just flour, water is just water.
Nerea: Then why did you stay here for three years if you think it’s all just commodities?
Bosco: I stayed for the paycheck; now I’m leaving for a better one, so I have to go.
Nerea: You’re avoiding the question because you don’t have a respectful answer.
Bosco: I’m avoiding the conversation because my shift starts in four minutes.
Nerea: So if I post it, I’m making a mistake? Or just a business move?
Bosco: It’s your move, your mistake, your business; I’m out the back door.
Nerea: Fine. I’ll post it. Goodbye.
Bosco: Goodbye.

"I'm not in your position, so I'd make a different choice entirely." He slid the phone into his pocket and pulled it out again.

The oven fans rolled on. Nerea tightened her grip on the notebook, its corners damp. "That's a deflection. I'm paying rent on this space using this recipe. Is it theft of heritage?"

"Then why did you stay here for three years if you think it's all just commodities?"

Nerea stepped toward the pass-through. "You're avoiding the question because you don't have a respectful answer."

"Goodbye." The door swung shut behind him.

The sugar shack is a humid, wooden box smelling of boiling maple and wet wool. Outside, the wind whips through bare maples; inside, the air is thick with steam that clings to eyelashes and hair. A massive propane burner roars beneath a double-tiered stainless steel evaporator, its heat radiating like a blast furnace. Condensation drips from the rafters in rhythmic, annoying splashes. Sienna stands close to the boiling sap, her notebook shielded by a piece of cardboard, eyes scanning the frothing liquid for signs of trouble. She needs to know why the syrup is sticking to the bottom of the front channel, turning black and bitter before it hits the flipper. She wants the technical fix: adjust the flame? Lower the feed rate? Scrape more aggressively?

Bogdan leans against the far wall, arms crossed, wearing a stained flannel shirt that hasn’t seen a washer in days. He is checking his phone, the screen’s blue light reflecting in his tired eyes. He doesn’t want to talk. He wants to go home and sleep. He views Sienna’s questions as an intrusion on his quiet time at the end of a long shift. He offers vague deflections, suggesting she read the manual or ask someone else, all while keeping his body angled toward the door. The conversation turns on two objects: the digital thermometer clipped to the side of the pan and the wooden scraper resting on the rim, both of which Sienna gestures toward while Bogdan ignores them.

Sienna: He left an hour ago. Is it the heat intensity or the flow rate?
Bogdan: Honestly, it’s probably just bad sap; you should call the supplier.
Sienna: The sap is fine, it’s the technique. Do I need to scrape the sides more?

Bogdan: Check the calibration sticker; I’m not an instrument technician.
Sienna: Sticker says good. Look, just tell me if I’m dumping too much cold sap.
Bogdan: Sounds like a feed-rate issue; look up PID controllers online.
Sienna: I don’t have a PID controller. Do I lower the flame before flipping?
Bogdan: Flame management is your call; I’m really gotta go now.
Sienna: If I don’t fix this, I ruin ten gallons. Lower or raise?
Bogdan: Can’t help with operations; talk to the safety officer tomorrow.
Sienna: There is no safety officer on weekends. Just give me a guess, please.
Bogdan: I don’t guess; I log off. Good luck with the burn.

story:
Steam clung to Sienna's eyelashes as she stood at the front channel, notebook shielded under a square of cardboard. The burner roared beneath the evaporator, and condensation dripped from the rafters in slow, irritating splashes. A dark film was creeping along the bottom of the pan. Across the room Bogdan leaned against the wall in a flannel shirt gone stiff at the cuffs, thumbing his phone, its blue light pooling in his tired eyes.

"Hey Bogdan, the syrup is scorching in the front channel again—what am I missing?"

He didn't look up. "Man, I'm just about to head out; maybe check the online forums?"

She wiped her forehead with the back of her glove. "I need a real-time answer; the batch is losing sugar right now."

His shoulder had already turned toward the door. "Yeah, hard to say from here; ask the guy who set up the burner."

"He left an hour ago. Is it the heat intensity or the flow rate?"

"Honestly, it's probably just bad sap; you should call the supplier." A drip landed on the brim of his cap and he ignored it.

Sienna dipped a finger toward the frothing liquid, thought better of it, and pulled back. "The sap is fine, it's the technique. Do I need to scrape the sides more?"

The wooden scraper lay on the rim of the pan, its handle darkening with damp. Bogdan's eyes stayed on his screen. "I don't scrape; I just drive away. Try the instructional video in the lobby."

"I've watched the video three times." She tipped her head at the digital thermometer clipped to the pan, its numbers flickering. "Is the thermometer reading accurate?"

"Check the calibration sticker; I'm not an instrument technician."

She leaned in and squinted at the faded label. "Sticker says good. Look, just tell me if I'm dumping too much cold sap."

He shifted his weight, boots scuffing the planks. "Sounds like a feed-rate issue; look up PID controllers online."

"I don't have a PID controller. Do I lower the flame before flipping?"

The phone went dark in his hand and he tucked it into his chest pocket. "Flame management is your call; I'm really gotta go now."

Behind her the foam climbed toward the lip of the channel. She grabbed the scraper and held it ready. "If I don't fix this, I ruin ten gallons. Lower or raise?"

He zipped his jacket to the throat. "Can't help with operations; talk to the safety officer tomorrow."

"There is no safety officer on weekends. Just give me a guess, please."

Bogdan pushed the door open and cold air rushed in, tearing the steam into ribbons. "I don't guess; I log off. Good luck with the burn."

The door banged shut. Sienna turned back to the pan, the scraper trembling slightly in her hand.

plan:
The scanning room is a windowless box of matte gray acoustic tiles and humming server racks, smelling faintly of isopropyl alcohol and warm plastic. A single ring light illuminates the central plinth, casting harsh shadows against the white walls. The air is recycled and still, save for the low thrum of the 3D scanner’s cooling fans. Jasmin stands rigid beside the plinth, her posture tight with the specific anxiety of a deadline approaching. She has just finished scanning a residual limb and needs immediate confirmation that the point cloud density meets the fabrication threshold. Her eyes are fixed on the monitor, which displays a wireframe model that looks suspiciously jagged at the distal end. She wants a binary verification—yes, it’s usable, or no, rescan now—so she can stop wasting daylight.

Kenji leans against the doorframe, one hip cocked, keys jingling softly in his palm. He is wearing a coat he hasn’t yet put on, suggesting he has already mentally left the building. His attention is fractured, darting from Jasmin to the exit sign, then to his watch. He resents the interruption; he was in the middle of packing up when she intercepted him. He offers no technical engagement, instead treating the question as an administrative hurdle to be bypassed. He deflects toward protocols, software manuals, or other staff members who are conveniently unavailable. The conversation turns on two concrete objects: the monitor displaying the low-resolution mesh, which Kenji refuses to look at directly, and the heavy manual binder on the desk labeled ‘Acquisition Standards,’ which he gestures toward with vague indifference rather than opening.

story:
Jasmin stood rigid beside the plinth, one hand on the scanner arm, her eyes on the monitor. The wireframe glowed against the gray tiles, jagged at its distal end, and the fans thrummed low in the still air that smelled of alcohol and warm plastic.

"Kenji, do you have a second to check if this scan has enough resolution for the socket?"

Kenji leaned in the doorframe, keys jingling in his palm, a coat draped over one arm. His eyes went to the exit sign. "I'm actually heading out, but you can check the specs in the manual on the desk."

She glanced at the binder labeled Acquisition Standards, fat and unopened. "I'm asking because the mesh looks jagged; the manual is fifty pages of theory."

He tilted his wrist and checked his watch. "If it looks jagged, the system flags it; just trust the software warning."

"There is no warning, just visual noise. Can you tell me if the point density is sufficient?"

"I don't interpret raw data; that's the fabrication lab's call, not mine."

Jasmin's thumb pressed the edge of the plinth. "The lab won't talk to me until I sign off on the scan quality first."

"Then you need a supervisor to co-sign; they're at the next floor's lab."

"No supervisor is available today. You ran the last calibration, didn't you?"

His keys stopped jingling, then started again. "I hit the start button; the technician actually validated the settings before I left."

"That was three hours ago. If I rescan now, do I lose the session metadata?"

"Metadata locks automatically; I'm not sure how the backend handles retries."

She turned from the screen at last. "So it's a hard loss? That's the critical detail I need."

"Honestly, ask the IT desk; they track the database logs, I don't." He shifted his weight to the other hip.

"IT is in another building. Just look at the Z-axis error bar for me."

"My eyes aren't calibrated for that; I'd rather not guess and be wrong."

The ring light buzzed faintly over the plinth. "It's either pass or fail, not a guess. Is the resolution under 0.1 millimeters?"

"I don't have the micrometer handy and I really need to leave now." He slid one arm into a coat sleeve and stopped there.

"If I fabricate with this, will the socket fit, or do I risk pressure points?"

"Clinical decisions aren't my scope; please consult the prosthetist on record."

Jasmin's jaw set. "The prosthetist is on lunch. I need your professional opinion on the data quality."

"My opinion is that you should have waited for the tech; I'm out."

She stepped between him and the desk, the monitor's glow behind her. "You're refusing to look at the screen?"

Kenji angled his face toward the hallway, the second sleeve still hanging empty. "Screen's bright, I'm blind, and the door's right there; good luck."

The door sighed shut behind him, and the fans went on thrumming over the jagged mesh.
